chapters.title: Chapter 3: Case Studies in Currency Wars

lessons.title: How Indian Markets React: Nifty, IT Exporters, and Oil Importers

body.text: The same global currency shock can crash the entire Nifty on day one, then make an IT exporter's next earnings call sound upbeat and an oil marketing company's sound grim, weeks later. Reading Indian markets through a currency war requires knowing which of those two very different reactions you're actually looking at.

children.text: The Two-Speed Reaction: Risk-Off First, Fundamentals Later

markDefs.definition: A broad shift in investor sentiment toward selling riskier assets, including emerging market equities as a whole, regardless of any individual stock's specific fundamentals, typically triggered by a global shock or rising uncertainty.

children.text: Every episode covered in this chapter, the 2015 yuan shock, the 2013 taper tantrum, the 2024 yen carry unwind, hit Indian markets in two distinct phases that move at completely different speeds. The first is a

move: FIIs sell Indian equities as part of a broad emerging-market retreat within days or even hours, dragging almost every Nifty constituent down together, IT exporters and oil importers included, regardless of whether the underlying shock actually helps or hurts their specific business.

The second phase takes weeks to quarters: as the dust settles, sector-specific fundamentals reassert themselves. A weaker rupee genuinely helps IT margins and genuinely hurts oil marketing company costs, and those effects show up in the following quarter's results long after the initial panic-driven, indiscriminate selloff has faded. Confusing the two phases, reading Day 2 panic selling as a verdict on Day 90 fundamentals, is one of the most common mistakes retail investors make around these events.

body.caption: Two Speeds, Two Very Different Logics

Hours to days

Weeks to quarters

body.title: Quick Check: Which Phase Are You Looking At?
body.question: A global currency shock hits on a Monday. By Wednesday, IT exporters, oil marketing companies and banks have all fallen 3 to 5% together on the Nifty, with no company-specific news released. What does this most likely reflect?
options: A carefully researched, sector-differentiated reassessment of each company's currency exposure
The risk-off phase, broad-based FII selling of Indian equities as an asset class, largely indifferent to individual sector fundamentals at this stage
Proof that the currency shock hurts every Indian sector equally over the long run
A sign the RBI has announced a specific defended exchange rate level
body.explanation: Uniform selling across sectors with no company-specific news in a 48-hour window is the signature of the risk-off phase, not a fundamentals-driven repricing. The sector-specific story, IT margin gains, OMC cost pain, plays out later and rarely moves every stock by the same amount at the same time.

children.text: Sector by Sector: Who Actually Wins, Who Actually Loses
IT Exporters: A Genuine Tailwind, With a Catch

As Chapter 2 covered, a weaker rupee genuinely expands IT services margins, since revenue is largely dollar-denominated and a large share of costs are rupee-denominated employee costs. But a global currency shock, especially one tied to fears of a US or global slowdown like the 2024 yen unwind, often coincides with exactly the environment where IT clients cut discretionary technology spending. The margin tailwind is real; whether it's enough to offset a genuine demand slowdown depends entirely on what's actually driving the currency shock in the first place.
Oil Marketing Companies: The Direct Cost Hit

markDefs.definition: The profit oil marketing companies earn on fuel sold at the pump, which gets compressed when the rupee cost of imported crude rises faster than they can pass the increase on to retail prices.

children.text: India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil needs, priced in dollars. A weaker rupee raises the landed cost of every barrel immediately, and oil marketing companies such as IOC, BPCL and HPCL absorb the squeeze on their

whenever they cannot pass the full cost increase through to pump prices quickly, whether for competitive or political reasons. Before petrol and diesel pricing was deregulated in 2014, this gap was formally called an under-recovery and was partly compensated by the government; today it shows up more directly as squeezed marketing margins and OMC earnings, since formal price controls on petrol and diesel have largely been removed.

body.title: Quantify the Direct FX Hit
body.prompt: Crude oil costs $80 a barrel. The rupee depreciates 5% against the dollar overnight with no change in the dollar price of crude. Approximately what percentage does the landed rupee cost of that crude increase, all else equal?
body.explanation: With the dollar price unchanged, a 5% rupee depreciation raises the rupee cost of the same barrel by approximately 5%, a direct, near one-to-one pass-through before considering any hedging, inventory timing, or retail price adjustments an OMC might use to soften the impact.

children.text: Gold and Jewellery: A Genuine Two-Sided Effect

A weaker rupee makes imported gold costlier for Indian jewellers, squeezing their input costs exactly like an oil importer. But gold is also a classic safe-haven asset during currency chaos and global uncertainty, meaning the same currency war episode that raises jewellers' costs can simultaneously boost underlying demand for gold as a hedge, a genuinely two-sided effect that doesn't resolve as cleanly one way as the oil or IT stories do.
Banks and NBFCs: Caught in the Risk-Off Crossfire

Banks tend to carry the heaviest weight in Nifty and the deepest FII ownership, which makes them disproportionately exposed to the risk-off phase specifically, even though a currency shock rarely changes their domestic loan book fundamentals directly. The more genuine fundamental exposure sits with companies carrying dollar-denominated external commercial borrowings, whose rupee cost of servicing that debt rises directly with rupee weakness, a real, lasting effect rather than a sentiment-driven one.

children.text: Markets don't just watch the currency shock itself, they watch the RBI's reaction to it. As Chapter 2's case study showed, the moment the market perceives the RBI is defending effectively, whether through visible spot intervention, confident public communication, or a creative tool like the 2013 FCNR(B) swap scheme, sentiment often improves well before the underlying global shock has actually resolved. This relief rally is itself part of the risk-off-then-recovery pattern, driven by confidence in the defense, not by any change in the original global trigger.

body.title: Reading a Live Currency Shock: A Quick Framework

columns.label: Ask this in the first 48 hours
points: Is this broad, indiscriminate selling (risk-off) or is it sector-specific?
Is the RBI visibly responding, and does it have the reserves to sustain a defense?
Is the underlying global shock about a genuine slowdown, or a narrower currency-specific event?

columns.label: Ask this over the following quarter
points: Which sectors actually have real currency-linked cost or revenue exposure?
Is the fundamental effect (IT margins, OMC costs) showing up in reported results as expected?
Has the underlying global driver resolved, worsened, or simply faded from headlines without resolving?

body.title: You Are Reviewing Your Portfolio Three Days Into a Global Currency Shock
body.scenario: A major central bank's policy surprise has triggered a sharp global risk-off move. Over three trading days, the Nifty has fallen 4%, with IT, oil marketing companies and banks all down by similar amounts. Your portfolio holds a large-cap IT exporter, an oil marketing company, and a private bank with negligible foreign currency borrowings.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's two-speed framework, what would you actually do with each of the three holdings right now, versus what you would wait to see over the coming quarter?
body.modelAnswer: Right now, at Day 3, all three stocks falling by similar amounts is the risk-off signature, not a verdict on any one company's fundamentals, so this is not the moment to make sector-differentiated decisions based on the price action alone. The bank, given negligible foreign currency borrowings, has the weakest fundamental linkage to the currency shock itself; its fall is almost purely a risk-off, index-weight effect, so unless you have a separate reason to sell, riding this out is reasonable. For the IT exporter and the oil marketing company, the real test comes over the following quarter: watch whether the IT company's margin commentary shows the expected rupee tailwind and whether management flags any demand softness tied to the same global event, and watch whether the OMC's marketing margins actually compress as crude costs rise, and how much of that gets passed through to pump prices. Making a call on any of the three today, based on three days of uniform selling, risks confusing the risk-off phase for the fundamental one this lesson has spent the whole time separating.

cards.definition: Broad investor selling of riskier assets, including EM equities as a class, largely regardless of individual company fundamentals.
The profit oil marketing companies earn on fuel sold at the pump, compressed when rupee costs rise faster than retail price pass-through.
The pattern where currency shocks hit Indian markets first through indiscriminate risk-off selling, then through slower, sector-specific fundamental repricing.
A market recovery driven by confidence in the RBI's visible defense of the rupee, distinct from any resolution of the underlying global shock.

points: Currency shocks hit Indian markets in two speeds: an immediate, broad, sector-indifferent risk-off selloff, followed by a slower fundamental repricing that actually differentiates winners from losers.

IT exporters get a genuine margin tailwind from rupee weakness, but a shock tied to global slowdown fears can offset it through weaker demand, making the net effect ambiguous rather than automatically positive.
Oil marketing companies face a direct, largely unavoidable cost hit from rupee weakness given India's roughly 85% crude import dependency, showing up as marketing margin compression.
Gold and jewellery sit in a genuine middle ground: costlier imported input, partly offset by safe-haven demand during the same currency chaos.
Banks and NBFCs often fall hardest in the immediate risk-off phase due to index weight and FII ownership, despite limited direct fundamental currency exposure unless they carry dollar debt.
The next and final lesson turns this analysis into an actual portfolio positioning framework for currency war risk, the practical payoff for everything covered across this course.

Sector reactions described here are general patterns, not guarantees, and India's crude import dependency figure is a widely cited approximation; verify current figures against government and RBI data before relying on them for investment decisions.
